paragraphs: Policy iteration alternates between estimating how well a decision rule performs and constructing a new rule from those estimates. This paper studies a model-free version in which policy evaluation uses Sarsa updates and a linear approximation to state-action values. A separate policy improvement operator turns the learned values into the next policy.

The main result is a conditional convergence guarantee. The improvement operator must produce soft policies, retaining some probability of alternative actions. It must also be Lipschitz continuous in the action values, with a sufficiently small constant. In plain language, changes in estimated values must not cause excessively large changes in the resulting policy.

Under those conditions, the algorithm converges to a unique solution from any starting policy. The guarantee therefore links stable learning to controlled policy updates, even when values are approximated. It establishes convergence to a unique solution under the stated assumptions; it does not identify that solution as an optimal policy.
neurips-2002-a-convergent-form-of-approx.tldr: Approximate policy iteration converges to a unique solution when its policy updates remain sufficiently smooth and exploratory.

paragraphs: A classifier may be easier to design and train if its input patterns are spread more evenly through their representation space. This paper investigates a transformation intended to produce that spreading. Called the Digital Antennal Lobe, it takes inspiration from a structure involved in the grasshopper's sense of smell.

The transformation runs a discrete-time dynamical system for a few steps. The authors analyze how it redistributes patterns and how its average behavior depends on a small number of design parameters. This connects the system's adjustable settings to the behavior of the resulting map, making parameter choice an explicit design question.

The paper also suggests adapting the initial parameters to obtain suitable rejection of noise. That matters because redistributing patterns is useful only insofar as the transformation also handles unwanted input variation appropriately. Simulations demonstrate the reported properties. The broader motivation is that distribution equalization may simplify classification; the abstract does not claim that every classifier or dataset necessarily benefits.
neurips-2002-a-digital-antennal-lobe-for.tldr: A biologically inspired dynamical map spreads input patterns, with analysis and simulations connecting its parameters to equalization and noise rejection.

paragraphs: Regression predicts a numerical output, but a prediction alone does not say how reliably it will stay close to the underlying function. This paper formulates regression around that reliability question. Its objective is to maximize a lower bound on the probability that future predictions fall within a specified error tolerance of the true regression function.

The resulting method, minimax probability machine regression, directly estimates this lower probability bound. The tolerance describes how much error is acceptable, while the bound expresses a conservative probability of meeting that tolerance. These quantities give the regression objective an explicit interpretation in terms of prediction accuracy and reliability.

The framework extends an existing minimax probability classification approach and uses Mercer kernels to construct nonlinear regression models. Tests on synthetic and real-world data support both the accuracy of the estimated probability bound and the effectiveness of the predictors. The bound concerns a probability of staying within tolerance, so it should not be read as a promise that every future prediction satisfies the tolerance.
neurips-2002-a-formulation-for-minimax-p.tldr: Minimax probability machine regression learns nonlinear predictors while directly estimating a lower bound on their probability of meeting an error tolerance.

paragraphs: People can achieve the same movement goal repeatedly without reproducing every detail of the movement. This paper explains how reliable outcomes can coexist with variable trajectories. Its central claim is that, under uncertainty, allowing variation in redundant dimensions can be the optimal control strategy. These are aspects of movement that can vary without preventing success.

The authors show that optimal feedback control laws for typical motor tasks follow a minimal intervention principle. A deviation from the average trajectory calls for correction only when it interferes with the task goal. Feedback therefore depends on the consequence of a deviation, rather than treating every departure from an average movement as an error.

The resulting behavior has variability shaped by the task's requirements and coordinated coupling among actuators. These two properties emerge together from the control strategy. The explanation makes movement variability part of successful control under uncertainty: some details remain flexible while feedback protects the aspects of movement that determine whether the goal is reached.
neurips-2002-a-minimal-intervention-prin.tldr: Optimal feedback control under uncertainty can allow harmless movement variation while correcting deviations that threaten the task goal.

paragraphs: This paper addresses separating sound sources when only one recorded mixture is available. Its approach uses the temporal structure of sounds as prior information. Before separation, it learns sets of time-domain basis filters that represent sources statistically efficiently, providing a vocabulary of patterns with which to explain the mixed recording.

Given these filters and the observed recording, the authors derive a maximum-likelihood learning algorithm. At each time point, it infers the source signals and factors describing their contributions. The inference relies on both the previously learned filters and probability distributions for their coefficients. A flexible density model helps represent the observed data accurately.

Experiments report a high level of separation performance for mixtures of two music signals and for two voice signals. These results support using learned temporal structure to distinguish sources from a single channel. The role of prior information is central: the method's ability to infer separate signals depends on the basis filters and their associated coefficient distributions.
neurips-2002-a-probabilistic-approach-to.tldr: Learned temporal filters and coefficient distributions enable probabilistic separation of two sound sources from a single recorded mixture.

paragraphs: Speech and music have structure in how their frequency content changes over time. This paper uses that structure as prior knowledge in a Bayesian approach to audio enhancement. The authors construct a probabilistic model and prior distributions that can account for characteristic time-frequency patterns in audio waveforms.

Combining those priors with the observed signal produces a posterior distribution describing the quantities to be estimated. The authors use Markov chain Monte Carlo methods to draw samples from that posterior. This makes the learned estimate depend on both the recording and assumptions about plausible sound structure, with inference carried out through sampling.

The reported speech enhancement results compare favorably on objective measures with standard time-varying filters. In several cases, the method also performs better both objectively and subjectively. A particularly relevant feature is that these results do not assume advance knowledge of the noise power. The evidence supports the value of structured audio priors without claiming superiority in every tested situation.
neurips-2002-bayesian-estimation-of-time.tldr: Bayesian time-frequency modeling improves speech enhancement in reported comparisons without requiring prior knowledge of noise power.

paragraphs: Image super-resolution combines several low-resolution observations into one higher-quality image. This requires determining how the observations align and how the unknown image was transformed into each observation. The reconstruction is ill-posed, so additional structure is needed to resolve ambiguities in the possible high-resolution images.

The paper develops a Bayesian treatment in which the likelihood for alignment parameters averages over the unknown high-resolution image. This marginalization accounts for possible images when assessing registration parameters. A Gaussian process prior over images makes the calculation tractable, and the approach also permits estimation of the unknown point spread function, which describes the imaging blur.

The reported results indicate a significant improvement over methods that optimize a single maximum-a-posteriori estimate of both the image and registration parameters. The central methodological contribution is therefore the treatment of image uncertainty during registration. Rather than committing immediately to one reconstructed image, the method uses an average over possible images to support estimation of the transformations and blur.
neurips-2002-bayesian-image-super-resolu.tldr: A Bayesian super-resolution method averages over unknown images when estimating alignment and can also infer blur, improving reported reconstruction results.

paragraphs: Inductive generalization concerns how people extend what they have observed to cases they have not seen. The authors argue that Bayesian reasoning provides a better explanation of this process than traditional accounts based on similarity calculations. Their approach treats generalization as reasoning over candidate hypotheses about what the observations imply.

The paper introduces an unsupervised method for constructing flexible hypothesis spaces. This addresses how the collection of candidate explanations can be formed, rather than simply assuming a fixed collection is already available. Flexible spaces also require a way to avoid conclusions that extend either too narrowly or too broadly beyond the evidence.

To address that issue, the authors propose a Bayesian Occam's razor that balances prior beliefs with how well hypotheses explain observations. They examine two previously published datasets on inductive reasoning and a new behavioral study. The contribution combines a way to construct candidate hypotheses with a principle for weighing them, grounding the proposed account in analyses of human generalization behavior.
neurips-2002-bayesian-models-of-inductiv.tldr: The paper proposes a Bayesian account of human generalization that learns flexible hypothesis spaces and balances evidence against prior beliefs.

paragraphs: Data described by many measurements can lie on an underlying surface with far fewer dimensions. This paper constructs a nonlinear mapping from the original sample space into a smaller vector space. The aim is to recover a Cartesian coordinate system for the manifold from which the observations were sampled.

The method first estimates the manifold's intrinsic dimensionality from samples. It then divides the data into low-dimensional patches that are locally linear and merges those patches into one coordinate system. This local-to-global construction preserves nearby geometric relationships while providing a shared representation across the sampled manifold.

The authors also compute mappings in both directions between the sample space and the coordinate space. They describe the mapping as pseudo-invertible, supporting a reverse map without asserting an unrestricted exact inverse. The objective functions are convex and have closed-form solutions. Together, these properties make the contribution a method for constructing and navigating a compact coordinate representation, with explicitly solvable optimization problems underlying the construction.
neurips-2002-charting-a-manifold-34ed21b.tldr: Locally linear patches are combined into a compact manifold coordinate system with forward and reverse mappings and closed-form optimization solutions.

paragraphs: Classification and ranking both involve expressing preferences among possible outputs. This paper presents a distance-based conditional model on a ranking poset, an ordered mathematical structure for rankings. The model extends the Mallows model and provides a framework for studying classification and ranking within the same probabilistic construction.

A central contribution is showing how the framework generalizes combination methods used in several learning algorithms. These include error-correcting output codes, discrete AdaBoost, logistic regression, and cranking. Bringing these methods into one model makes their relationships explicit rather than treating each combination rule as a separate construction.

The algebraic structure also gives the conditional model and its special cases a simple Bayesian interpretation. In particular, the framework suggests a probabilistic reading of error-correcting output codes and a way to extend them beyond binary coding. The stated contribution is thus both explanatory and constructive: it unifies existing methods and indicates a broader family of output representations for classification.
neurips-2002-conditional-models-on-the-r.tldr: A probabilistic model over rankings unifies several classifier combination methods and suggests output codes beyond binary schemes.

paragraphs: Dynamic Bayesian networks describe systems that evolve over time using observed and hidden variables. A major computational difficulty is averaging over the possible hidden variables. To keep this manageable, models commonly restrict the hidden representation to a small size or use Gaussian conditional distributions with linear dependence on previous states.

This paper proposes a different restriction: deterministic conditional probability tables for the hidden variables. These tables make the latent relationships deterministic within the model. That specialization changes which parts of the network need to carry complexity and permits tractable inference even when the observed-variable conditional distributions are highly nonlinear and non-Gaussian.

The result is a way to represent complex latent dynamics while retaining a manageable probabilistic model. Its significance lies in the particular modeling tradeoff: deterministic hidden relationships permit greater flexibility in the visible distributions. The tractability claim is tied to this specialization, so it should be understood as a property of the proposed model class rather than of unrestricted dynamic Bayesian networks.
neurips-2002-dynamic-bayesian-networks-w.tldr: Deterministic hidden-variable tables make inference tractable while allowing complex dynamics and nonlinear, non-Gaussian observation models.

paragraphs: The paper examines whether precise sequences of neural spike times could support cortical computation. Its starting requirement is robustness: if a computation depends on timing, perturbations must not make that timing unreliable. This turns a question about neural information processing into a question about the stability of network dynamics.

The authors draw on a framework that supplies a simple criterion for deciding whether a network's spike sequence is sensitive to its initial conditions. They combine this criterion with numerical simulations of several network architectures. The analysis therefore considers both a general stability test and examples of how networks behave under the modeled dynamics.

Within the limits of their neuron model, the authors argue that computation using precise spike-time sequences is unlikely under conditions typically encountered in cortex. This is a qualified argument about a particular computational possibility. Its force comes from the robustness requirement and the modeled dynamical behavior; it does not establish that all uses of neural timing are impossible.
neurips-2002-dynamical-constraints-on-co.tldr: Stability analysis and simulations suggest, within the neuron model studied, that precise spike-time sequences are unlikely to support computation under typical cortical conditions.

paragraphs: A partially observable decision problem requires planning with beliefs about the system's state. Standard value-function methods become intractable for large models partly because they seek an optimal policy across the whole belief space. This paper exploits the observation that many possible beliefs are unlikely, while plausible beliefs occupy a structured, lower-dimensional region.

The authors use exponential-family principal components analysis to compress belief states into learned features. The resulting representation replaces a sparse, high-dimensional belief space with a compact description of its relevant structure. Planning then takes place directly in this lower-dimensional feature space, making belief compression part of the decision-making procedure.

The paper reports that this approach can find policies for problems orders of magnitude larger than conventional techniques can handle. It demonstrates the algorithm on a synthetic problem and a mobile robot navigation task. The central premise is the low-dimensional structure of plausible beliefs: exploiting that structure reduces the space over which planning must operate.
neurips-2002-exponential-family-pca-for-.tldr: Compressing plausible belief states into learned low-dimensional features enables planning for substantially larger partially observable decision problems.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a statistical estimator that combines nonlinear regression with factor analysis. It approximately represents a rectangular data matrix through two low-rank matrices and three link functions. The link functions transform the factors and their combined representation, allowing the same basic decomposition to express different relationships in the data.

The framework includes principal components analysis, exponential-family PCA, the infomax version of independent components analysis, linear regression, and generalized linear models as special cases. This breadth matters because methods usually presented separately can be described through a common construction. The framework also contains additional cases, one of which the paper develops.

The authors provide an iterative procedure for optimizing the model parameters. For some established special cases, this procedure reduces to familiar algorithms; for other cases, it produces new algorithms. The contribution is therefore a shared language for several statistical models together with an optimization approach that spans them, rather than a claim that one configuration is best for every dataset.
neurips-2002-generalized2-linear2-models.tldr: Generalized² Linear² Models unify several regression and factorization methods through low-rank matrices, link functions, and a shared iterative optimization procedure.

paragraphs: A common way to describe an auditory neuron's response is through its spectrotemporal receptive field, or STRF. This model predicts responses as a linear function of a sound's spectrogram, which represents frequency content over time. The paper asks how much of early auditory cortical activity such a model can explain.

The authors develop a method for measuring the fraction of stimulus-related response power that a chosen type of stimulus-response model captures across a population. Focusing on stimulus-related power makes the question specifically about the response associated with the sound. The method provides a quantitative way to evaluate a model family's explanatory reach.

Applied to the layers of primary auditory cortex that receive thalamic input, the analysis finds that STRF models explain no more than 40% of stimulus-related response power. This places a substantial limit on the linear spectrogram description in the population examined. It shows that even these early cortical processing stages contain sound-related response structure that the tested linear models do not capture.
neurips-2002-how-linear-are-auditory-cor.tldr: Linear spectrogram models explain no more than 40% of stimulus-related response power in the auditory cortical layers examined.

paragraphs: A web page's words are only one source of evidence about its category. Links within a website and the organization of hub pages also carry structure. This paper uses those signals to improve a simple page classifier when it encounters a new website, exploiting that site's unlabeled pages through a variant of co-training.

The process begins with labels assigned by a bag-of-words classifier. A restricted wrapper learner uses those labels to propose patterns for identifying main-category anchors on hub pages. A third learner then uses the proposed wrappers as features, seeking a categorization that supports a simple hub structure while largely agreeing with the original classifier.

On real-world test cases, the technique significantly improves accuracy and reduces the error rate by about half on average. The result supports adapting page classifications through site organization as well as text. The learners connect preliminary labels to structural patterns, then use those patterns to refine the categorization of the unfamiliar site.
neurips-2002-improving-a-page-classifier.tldr: Using hub-page structure and internal links to adapt a text classifier roughly halves average error on the reported unseen-site tests.

paragraphs: This paper develops an incremental training strategy for the relevance vector machine, a Bayesian model with sparse solutions. The strategy operates on a subset of active basis functions rather than maintaining a large active representation throughout training. Sparsity keeps the number of these functions, and therefore computational complexity, low.

The authors formalize the strategy as a variant of expectation-maximization called Subspace EM. They also introduce a mean-field treatment of the classification model, whose exact inference is intractable. This approximation includes the Laplace approximation as a special case and is expected to provide a close approximation to exact Bayesian inference.

The algorithms are tested on two large datasets, with sizes on the order of thousands to tens of thousands of examples. The reported results indicate that Bayesian learning at this scale, including on MNIST, is realistic. The contribution combines computational savings from a sparse active representation with approximate inference for classification; the expected quality of the approximation remains distinct from an exact-inference guarantee.
neurips-2002-incremental-gaussian-proces.tldr: Incremental sparse training and mean-field classification inference make Bayesian learning practical on the larger datasets studied.

paragraphs: A classifier can receive information from labeled examples and from prior knowledge about which inputs belong to each category. This paper incorporates such knowledge into a linear support vector machine. The knowledge is expressed as multiple polyhedral regions, each associated with one of the two classes, giving it a geometric form the classifier can use.

The authors reformulate the learning problem so that incorporating these regions leads to a linear program that can be solved efficiently. This provides a direct route from structured prior knowledge to a learned decision boundary. It also makes it possible to refine how the supplied knowledge is applied through the classifier formulation.

Examples involving DNA sequencing and breast cancer prognosis demonstrate the method, with reported improvements in test accuracy after prior knowledge is added. In one experiment, a linear classifier built solely from prior knowledge substantially outperforms direct application of the corresponding rules. That finding shows that the form in which knowledge is used can matter, alongside whether training examples are available.
neurips-2002-knowledge-based-support-vec.tldr: Encoding prior knowledge as class-associated geometric regions improves linear SVM test accuracy in the reported applications.

paragraphs: Bag-of-words representations describe documents through their terms but do not directly capture similarity in meaning between different terms. This paper proposes two ways to infer semantic similarity from a corpus. Both methods produce kernel functions, making the resulting similarities usable in kernel-based learning methods such as support vector machines.

The first method makes word similarity and document similarity depend on each other. Similar documents help establish relationships between words, while related words help establish relationships between documents. The authors express this mutual dependence as a system of equations and use its equilibrium to define similarity. The second method uses diffusion on a graph built from lexicon and co-occurrence information.

Each approach yields a family of valid kernels controlled by a real-valued parameter. The paper shows that an alignment measure can successfully guide selection of this parameter. Combined with support vector machines, the approaches produce positive results. Their shared contribution is to turn corpus-derived semantic relationships into a tunable similarity measure that a classifier can use.
neurips-2002-learning-semantic-similarit.tldr: Two corpus-based methods learn semantic similarity kernels through mutual word-document relationships or graph diffusion, with positive SVM results.

paragraphs: Information retrieval connects a user's query with documents judged relevant to it. This paper studies an explicit parametric probabilistic model of documents, queries, and relevance assessments. Placing these elements within one model makes parameter estimation a central part of learning how the retrieval system should relate queries to documents.

The authors apply mean-field methods to analyze the model and derive efficient practical algorithms for estimating its parameters. They also address hyperparameters, which govern the model or estimation procedure. These are selected using a fast approximation to leave-one-out cross-validation based on the cavity method, connecting model fitting with a separate mechanism for choosing its higher-level settings.

The resulting algorithm is evaluated on several benchmark databases against standard information retrieval algorithms. The abstract reports the evaluation but does not specify a comparative performance outcome. The methodological contribution is the combination of an explicit retrieval model, efficient approximate parameter estimation, and a fast approximate validation procedure for selecting hyperparameters.
neurips-2002-mean-field-approach-to-a-pr.tldr: Mean-field inference and approximate cross-validation provide practical parameter and hyperparameter estimation for a probabilistic information retrieval model.

paragraphs: This paper approaches multiclass classification by learning representations for both examples and class labels. Two embeddings place them in a common space, and an example receives the label located nearest to it. Classification therefore depends on the geometry of the learned representations and on how the two mappings fit together.

The authors introduce and analyze Bunching, an algorithm that learns this pair of embeddings from labeled data. A central element of the analysis is probabilistic output codes, which generalize error-correcting output codes. This construction broadens the coding framework while retaining a connection to an established approach to multiclass learning.

The paper shows that multiclass categorization with error-correcting output codes is a special case of Bunching. Comparisons across numerous categorization problems demonstrate an advantage for Bunching over that method. The findings support learning within the broader framework on the problems studied, while the special-case relationship explains precisely how the new approach encompasses an existing one.
neurips-2002-multiclass-learning-by-prob.tldr: Bunching learns a shared space for examples and labels, generalizing error-correcting output codes and outperforming them in reported comparisons.

paragraphs: This paper studies particle filtering for diagnosing faults in industrial processes. Particle filters represent possible process conditions through a collection of samples, so their usefulness depends on how effectively those samples support inference. The authors investigate this issue in two applications: an industrial dryer and a level tank.

They compare standard particle filtering, Rao-Blackwellised particle filtering, and a Rao-Blackwellised variant that looks one step ahead to choose promising sampling regions. The comparison asks whether spending more computation on each particle is worthwhile. In particular, the look-ahead method uses additional processing to guide where samples are placed.

For these applications, the authors report that reduced error and variance more than compensate for the extra processing required by the sophisticated methods. This finding makes computational cost per particle only part of the efficiency picture. A more expensive particle can still be useful overall when the resulting inference is more accurate and less variable, as observed in the two process-monitoring settings studied.
neurips-2002-real-time-monitoring-of-com.tldr: More sophisticated particle filters reduce error and variance enough to justify their extra processing in two industrial fault-diagnosis applications.

paragraphs: This paper translates ideas from vertebrate retinal processing into a programmable analog array processor. The model imitates aspects of how images are processed along the visual pathway. Its purpose is to support early vision applications through hardware capable of complex dynamics across both space and time.

The authors designed and fabricated a two-layer prototype chip using a standard 0.5-micrometer CMOS process. This establishes a physical implementation of the proposed model. Programmability matters because the chip's spatiotemporal behavior can be configured, allowing the retinally inspired architecture to serve as a platform for different processing dynamics.

The abstract reports computing capability relative to chip area and power consumption among the highest reported for a single chip. The paper also presents design challenges, tradeoffs, and experimental results. Taken together, the contribution connects a biological processing model to an implemented hardware architecture, supporting its feasibility as an alternative for early vision in standard semiconductor technology.
neurips-2002-retinal-processing-emulatio.tldr: A fabricated programmable analog chip implements retina-inspired spatiotemporal processing for early vision applications.

paragraphs: Simple sounds such as clicks and brief tones are easy to interpret experimentally, but they may miss complex neural response properties. This study instead probes rat auditory cortex with richer sounds, including animal vocalizations and music. It uses in vivo whole-cell recordings to measure membrane-potential fluctuations below the threshold for producing spikes.

These recordings reveal synaptic input to a neuron, providing a richer view than its sparse sequence of output spikes alone. Many neurons respond robustly and reliably to the complex stimuli. The authors analyze the linear part of the relationship between each sound's time-varying spectrogram and the recorded membrane potential through spectrotemporal receptive fields.

The receptive fields show rich temporal structure, with excitatory regions generally consistent with simple tuning-curve predictions. Yet in many cases, substantial stimulus-determined responses cannot be predicted by the linear component. This combination shows both the usefulness and the limits of the linear description: it captures meaningful response organization while leaving nonlinear properties that remain uncharacterized.
neurips-2002-spectro-temporal-receptive-.tldr: Whole-cell recordings reveal reliable responses to complex sounds, with substantial nonlinear structure beyond what linear receptive fields predict.

paragraphs: Variational methods support approximate inference and learning in probabilistic models, but applying them often requires substantial manual work. For each application, researchers must derive update equations and implement specialized code. This paper introduces VIBES, an inference engine intended to automate both steps and reduce their time cost and susceptibility to errors.

Users specify a model through a simple script or a graphical interface resembling a drawing tool. VIBES then generates the corresponding variational equations and solves them automatically. This separates describing a probabilistic model from writing the mathematical updates and application-specific implementation needed to perform inference.

The authors illustrate the system's flexibility with examples from Bayesian mixture modeling. The contribution is a general-purpose route to variational solutions for a wide variety of models, making model specification the main user-facing task. Its scope remains variational inference: automating the equations provides an approximate-inference workflow, rather than changing those approximations into exact Bayesian calculations.
neurips-2002-vibes-a-variational-inferen.tldr: VIBES automatically derives and solves variational inference equations from scripted or graphical Bayesian-network specifications.
